research.notes: RESOLVED (the Wave-1 cross-family uncertainty): mutable/dynamic NFTs ARE live on XRPL mainnet. The DynamicNFT amendment (standard XLS-46d, XRPL-Standards discussion #130; amendment hash C1CE18F2A268E6A849C27B3DE485006771B4C01B2FCEC4F18356FE92ECD6BB74) was introduced in rippled 2.4.0 and ENABLED ON MAINNET 2025-06-11 (activation coincided with the Apex 2025 summit). The exact, narrow scope as of mid-2026: ONLY the URI field of an NFToken can change after mint, and only if the NFT was minted with the tfMutable flag (0x00000010). Mutation is performed by the new NFTokenModify transaction, callable ONLY by the issuer or the issuer's authorized minter -- never the current holder. Everything else (Flags, Issuer, NFTokenTaxon, TransferFee, the NFTokenID itself) remains permanently immutable, as it always has been under XLS-20. There is NO general 'dynamic NFT' (no on-chain stat fields, no holder-driven mutation); the standard pattern is URI -> off-chain JSON metadata where the JSON (and the art it points to) carries the evolving state. For game items the canonical evolving-gear loop is: mint tfMutable -> on level-up the issuer/minter swaps the URI to point at the new metadata document (new tier art + stats). When mutability is NOT desired or available (legacy XLS-20 NFTs minted before the amendment, or NFTs minted without tfMutable), the only path to 'change' an item is burn (tfBurnable) + remint -- which changes the NFTokenID and breaks provenance/offers, and historically risked sequence collisions until fixNFTokenRemint introduced FirstNFTSequence. Builder takeaway: design game items as tfMutable dNFTs with a stable URI pattern from day one; off-chain metadata mutability is free and instant but centralized (you control the document), on-chain URI mutability is the trust anchor that proves the issuer authorized the change.

capabilities.name: DynamicNFT Amendment
capabilities.summary: The protocol amendment that makes mutable NFTs possible on XRPL. It adds the NFTokenModify transaction and the tfMutable mint flag, allowing an NFToken's URI field to be changed after minting. This is THE answer to the Wave-1 'is dynamic NFT live?' question: yes, on mainnet, with a deliberately narrow scope (URI only). Without this amendment all NFToken fields were permanently frozen at mint.
capabilities.key_fields: Amendment hash C1CE18F2A268E6A849C27B3DE485006771B4C01B2FCEC4F18356FE92ECD6BB74; introduced rippled 2.4.0; standard XLS-46d (discussion #130); adds NFTokenModify tx type + tfMutable (0x00000010) tx flag + lsfMutable (0x0010) ledger flag.
capabilities.gotchas: Scope is far narrower than the marketing term 'dynamic NFT' implies -- it does NOT add on-chain stat fields or holder-driven mutation; it ONLY unlocks URI rewrites. NFTs minted before 2025-06-11 (or after, without tfMutable) are NOT retroactively mutable -- the flag must be set at mint and cannot be added later. An amendment can technically be re-disabled by validator vote, but it has held supermajority since activation.

capabilities.name: NFTokenModify Transaction
capabilities.summary: The transaction that actually performs the mutation: it updates (or deletes) the URI field of a mutable NFToken. This is the on-chain action a game backend submits when an item levels up or changes state -- the issuer (or authorized minter) rewrites the URI to point at the new metadata document. It is the single mechanism for true on-chain mutability of game items on XRPL.
capabilities.key_fields: Account (Address, required -- must be issuer or authorized minter); NFTokenID (Hex/UInt256, required -- the NFT to modify); Owner (Address, optional -- the NFT's current holder, omit if same as Account); URI (Hex Blob, optional, up to 256 bytes -- the new value; OMITTING the URI DELETES the existing URI). No validation is performed on URI content.
capabilities.gotchas: ONLY the issuer or authorized minter can submit it -- the current holder CANNOT mutate their own item (deliberate: prevents counterfeiting/self-upgrade). Fails with tecNO_PERMISSION if the NFT was not minted tfMutable or the Account is neither issuer nor authorized minter. Omitting URI silently deletes it rather than leaving it unchanged -- always resend the full intended URI. URI cap is 256 bytes, so store a pointer (IPFS CID / HTTPS URL), never inline metadata. Owner field is required when the NFT is held by someone other than the issuer.

capabilities.name: tfMutable Mint Flag
capabilities.summary: The mint-time decision that makes (or forever forecloses) an NFT's mutability. tfMutable (0x00000010) is set in the Flags field of NFTokenMint; it persists on the ledger object as lsfMutable (0x0010). This is a one-shot, irreversible design choice: an NFT minted without tfMutable can NEVER become mutable, and one minted with it is permanently eligible for NFTokenModify. For a game studio this is the most important line of code in the minting pipeline.
capabilities.key_fields: tfMutable transaction flag = 0x00000010 (decimal 16), set in NFTokenMint.Flags; corresponds to ledger flag lsfMutable = 0x0010 on the NFToken object. Sits alongside tfBurnable (0x00000001), tfOnlyXRP (0x00000002), tfTransferable (0x00000008).
capabilities.gotchas: Decision is permanent and cannot be retrofitted -- you cannot add mutability to an already-minted NFT, full stop. The transaction-flag value (0x00000010) and the ledger-flag value (0x0010) differ in width; don't confuse them when reading vs writing. Combine flags with bitwise OR (e.g. tfTransferable | tfMutable = 0x18) -- a common mint for tradeable evolving gear. Marketplaces/wallets should display the lsfMutable flag so buyers know an item's art/stats can change under them; not all UIs surfaced this immediately after activation.

capabilities.name: URI-Only Mutability Boundary
capabilities.network_status: Reflects current mainnet behavior as of mid-2026 (post DynamicNFT). Definitive scope of what can/can't change.
capabilities.summary: The precise answer to 'what exactly is mutable?' -- ONLY the URI field. Everything else on an NFToken is frozen at mint forever: Flags, Issuer, NFTokenTaxon, TransferFee, and the NFTokenID itself. There are no native on-chain stat/attribute fields to mutate. This boundary is the single most important design constraint for evolving game items on XRPL: all evolving state must live behind the URI (in off-chain metadata), never in NFToken fields.
capabilities.key_fields: Mutable: URI (256-byte Hex Blob, via NFTokenModify). Immutable forever: Flags, Issuer, NFTokenTaxon (collection/series id), TransferFee (royalty 0-50000 = 0-50%), Sequence, and the composite NFTokenID (Flags|TransferFee|Issuer|Taxon|Sequence).
capabilities.gotchas: You cannot change royalty (TransferFee) or move an item between collections (Taxon) post-mint -- bake these into mint correctly. The NFTokenID is content-addressed from immutable fields, so it never changes even when URI does -- good for stable references, but means the ID alone tells a marketplace nothing about current state (it must re-fetch the URI). Because only a pointer changes, 'mutability' is really 'repointing' -- the integrity of evolution depends entirely on how trustworthy the off-chain target is.

capabilities.name: Evolving / Leveling Game-Item Pattern (dNFT)
capabilities.network_status: Buildable on Mainnet today (depends on DynamicNFT, live 2025-06-11). Pattern-level guidance, not a single tx.
capabilities.summary: The canonical loop for leveling gear / state-changing items on XRPL. Mint each item with tfMutable and a stable URI scheme (e.g. ipfs://<cid>/item/<id> or https://api.studio/meta/<id>); when the player levels the item up, the studio backend (issuer or authorized minter) submits NFTokenModify to repoint the URI at the new tier's metadata (new art + stats). The NFTokenID is unchanged, so the player keeps the same on-chain asset, provenance, and any open offers -- only its appearance/attributes evolve.
capabilities.key_fields: Mint: NFTokenMint with Flags = tfTransferable|tfMutable, URI -> tier-0 metadata. Evolve: NFTokenModify {Account: issuer/minter, Owner: holder, NFTokenID, URI -> tier-N metadata}. Metadata JSON follows XLS-24d structure (name, image, attributes/stats).
capabilities.gotchas: The studio must keep the issuing (or authorized-minter) key online/secured to perform upgrades -- this is a centralization point and a key-custody risk. Players cannot self-upgrade (by design); the game logic must trigger the backend mutation. Wallets/marketplaces cache metadata -- evolved items may show stale art until a refresh; instruct UIs to re-fetch on a version/etag bump. If you want verifiable rarity caps, enforce 'max N upgrades' in your backend AND consider exposing the count in metadata, since the protocol does NOT limit modification frequency. Use an authorized minter (NFTokenMinter account setting) so the cold issuer key stays offline while a hot minter key does routine upgrades.

capabilities.name: Off-Chain Metadata vs On-Chain Mutability (XLS-24d)
capabilities.summary: The two distinct axes of 'changeability' a studio must reason about separately. (1) Off-chain metadata mutability: the URI points to a JSON document you host (HTTPS) or pin (IPFS); if it's HTTPS you can change the JSON/art ANYTIME with zero ledger txns and zero fees -- but it's centralized and unverifiable. (2) On-chain mutability: NFTokenModify changes the URI itself, leaving a signed, timestamped ledger record that the issuer authorized the change. The strongest game design uses both: an immutable IPFS pointer per tier, repointed on-chain at each level-up, so every evolution is provable AND content-addressed.
capabilities.key_fields: Metadata schema: XLS-24d (image, name, description, attributes/traits). URI transports: ipfs:// (content-addressed, immutable per CID), https:// (mutable in place), data: (RFC 2397 inline, capped by 256-byte URI limit).
capabilities.gotchas: HTTPS-mutable metadata means the studio can silently rewrite an item's stats/art with no ledger trace -- buyers can't trust it; reserve this only for non-economic cosmetic flexibility. Pure IPFS without on-chain modify means you must repin a NEW CID and run NFTokenModify to evolve (the CID changes when content changes) -- so IPFS evolution always costs an on-chain modify. The 256-byte URI cap forbids meaningful inline (data:) metadata for anything but trivial items. Decide per item class: collectibles/economic items -> IPFS + on-chain modify (provable); cosmetic-only -> HTTPS (cheap, flexible).

capabilities.name: Burn + Remint Fallback (fixNFTokenRemint)
capabilities.network_status: Live on Mainnet -- NFTokenBurn is part of base NFT support (NonFungibleTokensV1_1); fixNFTokenRemint enabled on Mainnet 2023-11-28 (FirstNFTSequence). This is the ONLY path to 'change' a non-mutable NFT.
capabilities.summary: The pre-DynamicNFT (and still-necessary-for-legacy) way to 'evolve' an item when true mutability isn't available: burn the old NFToken (requires tfBurnable or holder consent) and mint a fresh one with the new art/stats. It works on any NFT but is strictly inferior to dNFTs -- a new NFTokenID is created, severing provenance, open offers, and any external references. fixNFTokenRemint exists because naive remint risked reusing a sequence number and colliding with an old, still-cached NFTokenID; it added the FirstNFTSequence field to guarantee uniqueness.
capabilities.key_fields: NFTokenBurn {Account, NFTokenID, Owner?} then NFTokenMint {new URI, flags}. fixNFTokenRemint adds FirstNFTSequence to the issuer's AccountRoot so reminted tokens get fresh sequence numbers (no collision with previously-burned IDs).
capabilities.gotchas: Provenance breaks -- the new item is a different on-chain asset; collectors lose continuity and any marketplace history. Active buy/sell offers on the old NFT are destroyed with the burn. Burning requires either lsfBurnable set at mint (issuer-burnable) or the holder to burn their own -- you can't unilaterally burn a player's non-burnable item. Two transactions + fees per evolution vs one cheap NFTokenModify. Only choose this for legacy NFTs minted before DynamicNFT or without tfMutable; for any NEW game item, mint tfMutable and use NFTokenModify instead -- this fallback is a last resort, not a design default.

research.notes: Wave-2 depth synthesis (web-verified mid-2026). XRPL NFTs (XLS-20 family, NonFungibleTokensV1_1) trade through a native, escrowless offer book: every sale is an NFTokenCreateOffer object accepted by NFTokenAcceptOffer, with ownership and funds settling atomically in one ledger transaction so neither marketplace nor counterparty ever custodies the asset. The load-bearing architectural fact for a game studio is BROKERED MODE: an NFTokenAcceptOffer that names BOTH a sell offer and a buy offer lets a third-party broker match them and skim NFTokenBrokerFee from the spread WITHOUT ever owning the NFT or holding funds -- this is how every real XRPL marketplace (xrp.cafe ~1.589% broker fee, Sologenic 0% commission, xpmarket) inserts its cut. Royalties are enforced at Layer 1 via the immutable TransferFee minted into the NFT (units of 1/100,000; 0-50,000 = 0%-50%), and crucially the protocol pays the issuer FIRST out of the buyer's funds, then the broker, then the seller -- the broker-fee constraint is that the seller must still net at least the sell-offer amount BEFORE the transfer fee is applied. The royalty 'reality': XRPL's L1 enforcement is genuinely stronger than EVM marketplace-cooperation models, BUT it only binds on NATIVE NFTokenAcceptOffer transfers; an owner can still gift/move the NFT at a 0-price offer or via a side deal and re-list, so royalties bind sales-through-the-offer-book, not all economic transfers. A transfer-fee NFT can ONLY trade in a currency the issuer holds a trust line for (or be locked to XRP via the lsfOnlyXRP mint flag) -- for a game studio that means: mint with lsfTransferable + a TransferFee + (usually) lsfOnlyXRP, and design the in-game marketplace as a broker, not a custodian. Newer pieces shipped: NFTokenMintOffer (XLS-52, mainnet ~Feb 2025) collapses mint+list into one tx; DynamicNFT/tfMutable + NFTokenModify (mainnet ~Jun 2025) lets mutable game-asset URIs be upgraded post-mint; fixEnforceNFTokenTrustlineV2 closed a transfer-fee bypass against frozen/unauthorized trust lines. There is no native 'collection offer' (floor-sweep across a whole taxon) primitive yet -- marketplaces approximate it off-ledger by aggregating per-NFTokenID buy offers; the on-ledger NFTokenTaxon only groups a collection logically.

capabilities.summary: The core marketplace primitive: a single NFTokenAcceptOffer naming BOTH NFTokenSellOffer and NFTokenBuyOffer for the same NFTokenID, submitted by a broker who never owns the NFT. The broker keeps NFTokenBrokerFee from the spread between buy and sell prices; the NFT moves seller->buyer and funds settle atomically in one ledger transaction. This is how a studio inserts a marketplace fee without custody.

research.notes: Mid-2026 depth synthesis on how an XRPL game describes and hosts its asset data. The on-chain footprint is deliberately tiny: a minted NFToken (XLS-20, enabled mainnet 2022-10-31) carries a single URI field capped at 256 bytes, hex-encoded, with NO validity check by the protocol -- it can point to ipfs://, https://, arweave/ar://, magnet:, or an inline RFC-2397 data: URI. Everything a marketplace shows (name, image, traits, rarity, stats) lives OFF-chain in a JSON metadata document the URI resolves to. Two things changed the design space since launch: (1) the DynamicNFT amendment (XLS-46) went live on mainnet 2025-06-11, adding the tfMutable flag (0x0010, set ONLY at mint) plus the NFTokenModify transaction so the issuer/authorized minter can rewrite the URI of a mutable NFT -- this is the on-chain hook for evolving/leveling game items, though ONLY the URI changes, never other fields; (2) IPFS pinning economics shifted -- NFT.Storage Classic decommissioned new uploads 2024-06-30, pushing builders to Pinata, Lighthouse, and Storacha for hot IPFS, while Arweave remains the pay-once permanence option. The metadata schema layer is community convention, not protocol: XLS-24d ('Metadata Structure for XLS-20d NFTs', Discussion #69) is a DRAFT community standard with NO on-chain enforcement -- it explicitly names 'game_item' as a first-class NFT type and defines a type/name/description/creators/collection/properties shape where properties.attributes hold typed traits ({attribute_name,value_type,value}). In practice most XRPL marketplaces (Bithomp, xrpl.org tooling, xrplmeta, Sologenic, onXRP) also accept the OpenSea-style flat schema (name/description/image/attributes[{trait_type,value,display_type}]) because it maximizes cross-marketplace display. For a game, the durable pattern is: pick a stable off-chain JSON schema (OpenSea-compatible + a game_item extension), host immutable image/3D assets on Arweave or pinned IPFS with a CIDv1, point the NFToken URI at the JSON (also content-addressed), and use tfMutable + NFTokenModify only where item state must evolve. Marketplaces/wallets resolve metadata by reading the on-chain URI, fetching through an IPFS/Arweave gateway, then caching aggressively in their own indexer because direct gateway fetches are too slow for grid scrolling -- so metadata that mutates can lag in caches.

capabilities.name: NFToken URI field (XLS-20)
capabilities.summary: The URI field is the ONLY metadata-bearing field a native XRPL NFToken carries on-chain. It is an optional, variable-length blob capped at 256 bytes, stored hex-encoded (use convertStringToHex / similar). The protocol does NOT validate or dereference it: it can hold an ipfs:// CID, an https:// URL, an ar:// / Arweave gateway URL, a magnet link, or an inline RFC-2397 data: URI. It must not be an empty string if present. By default the URI is immutable for the life of the token -- it can only change if the NFToken was minted with the tfMutable flag (see DynamicNFT). Because 256 bytes is too small for real metadata, the URI is virtually always a pointer to an off-chain JSON document, not the metadata itself. This single field is the entire bridge between the on-chain token and everything a player/marketplace sees.

key_fields.validity_check: none -- protocol stores bytes verbatim, never fetches
key_fields.supported_schemes: ipfs://, https://, ar:// / Arweave gateway, magnet:, RFC-2397 data: URI
key_fields.mutability: immutable by default; mutable only if minted with tfMutable (0x0010)
key_fields.empty: field may be omitted, but must not be an empty string when present

capabilities.gotchas: 256 BYTES, not characters -- a long https URL plus query string can blow the budget; content-addressed ipfs:// CIDs are compact and the safer default. The URI is hex-encoded on the wire; forgetting to encode (or double-encoding) is a classic mint bug. The ledger never checks the link works, so a dead gateway = a permanently broken-looking NFT with no on-chain remedy unless tfMutable was set. The URI is immutable after mint UNLESS tfMutable was enabled AT mint -- you cannot retrofit mutability. Do NOT stuff raw metadata into the URI via data: in production: it bloats every ledger entry and you lose the 256-byte budget instantly.

capabilities.name: XLS-24d NFT metadata schema
capabilities.summary: XLS-24d ('Metadata Structure for XLS-20d NFTs', XRPLF/XRPL-Standards Discussion #69) is the XRPL-native community standard for the off-chain JSON document an NFToken URI points to. It is a DRAFT with NO on-chain enforcement -- nothing in the protocol validates it; it is a shared convention so marketplaces and galleries can render NFTs consistently. Notably it defines a top-level `type` field and explicitly lists `game_item` alongside `art`, `ticket`, and `general_purpose` as first-class NFT types -- directly relevant to a game studio. The shape is type/name/description/creators[]/collection/localization/properties, where `properties` holds the type-specific payload: primary_display (a file object), primary_animation, an `attributes` array of typed traits ({attribute_name, value_type, value} with value_type like string/decimal/int/vector), additional `files`, and expiration handling. It is more structured and type-aware than the OpenSea schema, but adoption across XRPL marketplaces is uneven, so most production NFTs pair or replace it with the OpenSea-style flat schema for maximum display compatibility.

capabilities.name: OpenSea-compatible NFT metadata schema
capabilities.summary: The de-facto JSON metadata schema that most NFT marketplaces and wallets -- including the XRPL ecosystem's Bithomp, Sologenic, onXRP/XPMarket, and xrpl.org-aligned tooling -- understand for free. Originating as the ERC-721/OpenSea metadata standard, it is a flat object: name, description, image (URI to the media), optional animation_url / external_url, and an `attributes` array of trait objects {trait_type, value, optional display_type, optional max_value}. display_type values like 'number', 'boost_number', 'boost_percentage', and 'date' tell a marketplace how to render numeric traits (e.g. show 'Damage 47' as a stat bar), and max_value bounds a trait for progress/ranking UI. For an XRPL game it is the safest single choice for guaranteed display because adoption is near-universal; the tradeoff is it is generic and not XRPL- or game-aware (no native type system). Common practice is to emit this schema (optionally with a nested game-item extension) so the asset shows everywhere, then layer richer structure where a specific marketplace supports it.

Rarity is NOT a field -- it is derived from trait frequency by indexers, so two marketplaces can compute different rarity ranks for the same NFT. Do not assume max_value enables on-chain leveling; it is purely a UI bound.

capabilities.name: Dynamic NFTs (tfMutable + NFTokenModify, XLS-46)
capabilities.summary: Dynamic NFTs (dNFTs) are the on-chain mechanism for changing an NFToken's metadata after mint, added by the DynamicNFT amendment (XLS-46), enabled on XRPL mainnet 2025-06-11 (rippled 2.4.x line). An NFT is made mutable by setting the tfMutable flag (0x0010) AT MINT TIME -- it cannot be added later and cannot be removed. Once mutable, the issuer or their authorized minter can send an NFTokenModify transaction to rewrite the URI field. Crucially, ONLY the URI can change -- never the issuer, taxon, transfer fee, flags, or NFTokenID. For a game this is the hook for evolving/leveling items, seasonal re-skins, fixing a dead asset link, or progressing state: mutate the URI to point at a new metadata JSON reflecting the new state. The pattern pairs naturally with content-addressed storage (each state = a new CID), giving an auditable on-chain trail of URI changes (every NFTokenModify is a ledger transaction).

key_fields.what_changes: URI field ONLY -- no other NFT property
key_fields.irreversibility: mutability cannot be added or removed after mint
key_fields.audit_trail: each URI change is a discrete on-chain NFTokenModify transaction

capabilities.gotchas: tfMutable MUST be decided at mint -- you cannot make an existing immutable NFT mutable later, and you cannot lock a mutable one. Only the URI changes; you CANNOT alter transfer fee, taxon, flags, or stats on-chain, so 'leveling up' really means swapping the off-chain metadata the URI points at. Mutability is a trust signal: holders/marketplaces know the issuer can rewrite the asset at any time, which can REDUCE perceived value/collectibility -- use it deliberately. Marketplace/wallet caches may serve STALE metadata after a NFTokenModify until they re-resolve, so a mutation isn't instantly visible everywhere. If you mutate the URI to a non-content-addressed location, you lose tamper-evidence; prefer a fresh CID per state.

capabilities.name: On-chain URI vs off-chain metadata hosting (pattern)
capabilities.summary: The core architectural split for every XRPL game asset: the ledger stores almost nothing (a hex URI <=256 bytes inside the NFToken), and ALL descriptive metadata + media lives off-chain at the resolved location. This is a deliberate cost/scalability tradeoff -- XRPL deliberately avoids fat on-chain blobs. The pattern that survives long-term: (1) host immutable media (sprites, portraits, 3D models) on content-addressed storage so the bytes can't silently change; (2) write a metadata JSON (OpenSea-compatible, optionally + game extension) that references those media URIs; (3) content-address the JSON too and put THAT URI on-chain; (4) reserve tfMutable+NFTokenModify only for assets whose state must evolve. The rare alternative -- a fully on-chain inline data: URI -- only fits trivially small SVG/text because of the 256-byte ceiling, so it is impractical for real game art. The off-chain choice is where permanence/mutability/cost tradeoffs (IPFS vs Arweave vs centralized) actually get made; the on-chain URI is just the pointer.

key_fields.on_chain: URI only, <=256 bytes hex, no validation, immutable unless tfMutable
key_fields.off_chain: metadata JSON + media (image/animation/3D) at the resolved URI
key_fields.content_addressing: ipfs:// CIDv1 or ar:// txid so bytes are tamper-evident
key_fields.json_then_media: URI -> JSON; JSON.image -> media URI (two hops)
key_fields.fully_on_chain_option: inline data: URI -- only viable for tiny SVG/text payloads
key_fields.permanence_decision: made off-chain (Arweave permanent vs IPFS pinned vs centralized)

capabilities.gotchas: An on-chain URI does NOT make your asset on-chain or permanent -- the token can outlive the host, leaving a valid NFT pointing at nothing (the #1 long-term NFT failure mode). HTTP(S) URLs are mutable and centralized: the issuer (or a hijacker) can swap what an immutable NFT 'shows' without any on-chain change -- content-addressing closes that hole. Two-hop resolution (URI->JSON->image) means BOTH hops must stay alive; pinning the JSON but not the image still breaks the asset. The 256-byte budget rules out fat on-chain metadata, so 'put it all on-chain' is not an option for game art. Plan media permanence at mint time -- there is no cheap retrofit for an immutable NFT whose host died.

capabilities.name: IPFS storage + pinning (service)
capabilities.summary: IPFS is the most common off-chain home for XRPL NFT media and metadata. Files are content-addressed by a CID (a hash of the bytes), so an ipfs:// URI is tamper-evident -- change the file and the CID changes, so an immutable NFToken URI can't silently point at altered art. The catch: IPFS does NOT guarantee permanence. Data persists only while at least one node PINS it; unpinned data is eventually garbage-collected and the link goes dead. So real use requires a pinning service. The landscape shifted: NFT.Storage Classic decommissioned new uploads on 2024-06-30 (existing data still served, with degrading latency), and the recommended hot-IPFS paths are now Pinata, Lighthouse, and Storacha; Filecoin/Lighthouse cover long-term durable backing. For a game studio IPFS is the pragmatic default for the bulk of immutable assets (sprites, portraits, item icons), giving content-addressing + low/variable cost, as long as you commit to keeping pins alive (or pay a service to).

capabilities.name: Arweave permanent storage (service)
capabilities.summary: Arweave is the pay-once, store-forever alternative to IPFS for XRPL NFT assets. Unlike IPFS, permanence is built into the protocol: you make a single upfront payment (in AR), and an endowment model funds ongoing replication on the 'blockweave' indefinitely -- no recurring pinning. Each upload gets a permanent, immutable transaction ID; the asset is referenced by an ar://<txid> or an Arweave gateway HTTPS URL, which (like IPFS CIDs) is effectively content-addressed and tamper-evident. As of 2026, storage runs roughly USD 0.002-0.005 per MB, so a few-MB image + tiny JSON is on the order of cents for permanent hosting. The classic tradeoff vs IPFS: Arweave has a higher per-byte upfront cost but ZERO ongoing operational burden and the strongest permanence guarantee, making it the better fit for a game's flagship/canonical immutable assets you must guarantee outlive any company. The common production answer is hybrid: Arweave (or pinned IPFS) for cold permanent originals, a fast CDN/gateway cache for hot delivery.

key_fields.permanence: protocol-level -- pay once, stored indefinitely via endowment model
key_fields.addressing: permanent immutable transaction ID; ar://<txid> or gateway HTTPS URL
key_fields.payment: single upfront fee in AR (no recurring pinning)
key_fields.tamper_evidence: txid is derived from content -- effectively content-addressed

key_fields.best_use: canonical immutable game originals; cold half of a hybrid setup

capabilities.gotchas: Permanence is also rigidity: you CANNOT delete or edit an Arweave upload -- a leaked or wrong asset is permanent, so vet before uploading. Higher upfront per-byte cost than starting an IPFS pin, so for huge/churning asset libraries the economics favor IPFS until you're storing for years/decades. ar:// is not natively resolved by most wallets/marketplaces -- you typically put the gateway HTTPS URL on-chain, which reintroduces a gateway dependency for display (the data itself stays permanent). Paying in AR adds a token-acquisition step vs a fiat IPFS subscription. Gateway latency still warrants a CDN cache for grid-heavy game UIs. Permanence guards the BYTES, not the link semantics -- a dNFT can still be modified to point away from a permanent asset.

capabilities.name: Game-item metadata schema (traits, rarity, stats)
capabilities.summary: The concrete pattern for modeling a game item (weapon, armor, consumable, character card) as NFT metadata that BOTH marketplaces and your game engine can read. Build on the OpenSea-compatible base (name/description/image/attributes) so the item displays everywhere, then encode game semantics through the attributes array and an optional namespaced extension: equipment stats as numeric traits with display_type:'boost_number' / 'boost_percentage' and a max_value bound (e.g. {trait_type:'Attack', value:47, display_type:'boost_number', max_value:100}); rarity/tier as an explicit categorical trait ({trait_type:'Rarity', value:'Legendary'}) since rarity is otherwise only inferred from trait frequency by indexers; slot/equip-type, level, element, and set membership as additional traits. For state that changes (leveling), pair this with tfMutable+NFTokenModify so each level = a new metadata JSON (ideally a new CID). The discriminator vs generic NFT art is that game items need an AUTHORITATIVE machine-readable contract for stats your engine trusts -- so define a fixed trait vocabulary (trait_type names, value ranges, enum tiers) and validate it, rather than relying on marketplace rendering.

key_fields.base: OpenSea schema: name, description, image, animation_url?, attributes[]
key_fields.stats: numeric traits w/ display_type boost_number|boost_percentage + max_value bound
key_fields.rarity: explicit categorical trait (Common..Legendary/Mythic) -- do not rely on frequency only
key_fields.slot_type_level: traits for equip slot, item type, level, element, set bonus
key_fields.extension: optional namespaced object (e.g. properties / game) for structured stats engines parse
key_fields.evolution: tfMutable + NFTokenModify -> new metadata JSON / CID per level/state
key_fields.contract: fixed trait vocabulary + value ranges + enum tiers, validated by the game

capabilities.gotchas: Marketplaces will RENDER traits but will NOT enforce your stat ranges or vocabulary -- the metadata is the source of truth and nothing stops a malformed or spoofed JSON, so your engine must validate against a schema, not trust the file. Rarity is not a protocol concept; different marketplaces compute different rarity ranks from trait frequency, so ship an explicit Rarity trait if rank matters to gameplay/economy. display_type is a hint a wallet may ignore -- don't depend on it for correctness, only presentation. If you put authoritative stats ONLY in a non-standard nested object, generic marketplaces show nothing useful; mirror key stats into flat attributes too. Mutating stats means re-issuing the JSON via NFTokenModify (URI-only) -- you can't change a stat 'in place', and caches may lag. Define and freeze your trait vocabulary early; renaming trait_type later splits filtering/rarity across old and new items.

capabilities.name: Marketplace / wallet metadata resolution & indexing
capabilities.summary: How an NFT actually gets DISPLAYED: a marketplace or wallet (Bithomp, Sologenic, onXRP/XPMarket, xrpl.org-aligned tooling) reads the NFToken's on-chain URI (via account_nfts / nft_info on rippled or a Clio server), hex-decodes it, fetches the resolved JSON through an IPFS/Arweave/HTTP gateway, then parses name/image/attributes and renders them. Because direct gateway fetches are far too slow for users scrolling pages of high-media NFTs, every serious marketplace CACHES the resolved metadata and media in its own indexer (Clio, the XRPL Data API / xrpldata, Bithomp's API, xrplmeta) -- so what you SEE is usually the cache, not a live fetch. This caching is the load-bearing fact for game builders: (1) trait-based filtering, rarity ranking, and collection grouping all happen in the INDEXER, so they depend on the schema you emit; (2) after a dNFT NFTokenModify the new metadata may not appear until the indexer re-resolves, sometimes with manual 'refresh metadata' needed; (3) collections are grouped by issuer + NFTokenTaxon, and issuer-level presentation (collection icon, social links) is read from the issuer's xrp-ledger.toml.

capabilities.gotchas: Caches go STALE: a dNFT you just modified can keep showing old art/stats until the indexer re-resolves, and some platforms need a manual 'refresh metadata' click -- never assume an NFTokenModify is instantly visible. Different indexers parse different schemas: a feature that shows on Bithomp may not on another marketplace, so test on the platforms your players use, not just one. Rarity rank is computed PER indexer from trait frequency, so the same NFT can rank differently across sites. If your URI points at a slow/rate-limited public gateway, first-resolution can fail or time out and the asset shows blank until retried -- use a fast/dedicated gateway and pin reliably. Collection identity hinges on a CONSISTENT issuer+taxon and a valid xrp-ledger.toml; an inconsistent taxon scatters your set across 'collections'. Indexers may not support every XLS-24d field -- emit OpenSea-compatible fields for the things you NEED displayed.

research.notes: Mid-2026 depth synthesis for NFT game-asset minting on XRPL (XLS-20). Wave 1 covered the primitives (NFTokenMint/Burn, basic offers); this wave goes deeper on the decisions a studio makes when issuing real collections at scale. Load-bearing 2026 facts: (1) DynamicNFT (NFTokenModify + tfMutable) is LIVE on mainnet since 2025-06-11 — mutable URIs are now a first-class option, decided irreversibly at mint time. (2) There is NO native on-chain 'collection' object; collection identity is the (Issuer, NFTokenTaxon) pair plus off-ledger metadata convention — taxon strategy is a design decision, not a feature you turn on. (3) The Batch amendment (XLS-56d) that would have enabled atomic multi-mint groups is NOT enabled on mainnet: a signature-validation vulnerability was found 2026-02-19 and rippled 3.1.1 (2026-02-23) marked Batch + fixBatchInnerSigs unsupported, so validators cannot vote it in until remediation lands. At-scale minting in mid-2026 therefore still relies on Tickets (parallel submission, ~200/group) + account-sequence pipelining, NOT atomic batches. (4) Reserve economics dominate large-collection design: each NFTokenPage holds up to 32 NFTs (assume ~24), costs one 0.2 XRP owner-reserve increment, so eager-minting N NFTs locks roughly N/12 XRP — for a 10k game collection that is ~833 XRP locked while unsold. Lazy/mint-on-demand sidesteps this entirely. (5) fixNFTokenRemint (live since 2023) makes NFTokenIDs derive from FirstNFTSequence + MintedNFTokens, which closes the delete-and-recreate ID-collision hole but also blocks issuer account deletion until FirstNFTSequence + MintedNFTokens + 256 < current ledger — a real operational footgun for studios that churn issuer accounts. (6) tfTrustLine is deprecated (fixRemoveNFTokenAutoTrustLine). Numbers verified against xrpl.org docs June 2026.

capabilities.name: NFTokenTaxon collection-identity strategy
capabilities.summary: XRPL has no native 'collection' ledger object. Collection identity is the pair (Issuer account, NFTokenTaxon) — every NFT minted by the same issuer with the same taxon is, by convention, one collection. The taxon is an arbitrary UInt32 the minter chooses, so taxon strategy (one collection = one taxon, vs sub-series/rarity tiers = distinct taxons, vs per-asset-type taxons for a game) is a deliberate design decision made at mint time and effectively permanent. Indexers, marketplaces, and your own game backend group by (issuer, taxon), so getting the scheme right up front is core to a game's asset taxonomy.
capabilities.key_fields: NFTokenTaxon (UInt32, required on NFTokenMint, range 0..4294967295; values >= 2147483648/0x80000000 are reserved by the protocol's scrambling — pick from the lower half to be safe). Collection = (Issuer, taxon). Taxon is scrambled inside the NFTokenID but the logical/unscrambled value is what you query on. There is no rename, no merge, no on-chain collection name/size/floor — those live off-ledger (metadata + marketplace). Sequence/serial within a collection comes from the NFTokenID's sequence component, set automatically per mint.
capabilities.gotchas: No way to change an NFT's taxon after mint — a mistaken taxon means a permanently mis-grouped asset, only fixable by burn+remint. Two different issuers can use the same taxon number with zero collision because identity includes the issuer account, but a single issuer reusing a taxon across what you intended as two collections silently merges them in every indexer. Don't encode rarity or stats in the taxon expecting tooling to parse it — taxon is opaque to the protocol; use the URI/metadata for that. Reserved taxon range (>=0x80000000) behaves oddly with scrambling; stay below it.

capabilities.name: Owner reserve & cost-per-NFT math (NFTokenPage packing)
capabilities.summary: An account's NFTs are stored in NFTokenPage objects, and the owner reserve is charged per page, NOT per NFT. Each page holds up to 32 NFTs (assume ~24 in practice due to ID-sorted packing), and each page costs one owner-reserve increment of 0.2 XRP. So the amortized cost of holding/minting N NFTs is roughly N/12 XRP. For a game studio this is the single most important number when deciding how big a collection to mint eagerly and who holds inventory — a 10,000-NFT eager mint locks ~833 XRP in reserve until those tokens leave the issuer's account.
capabilities.key_fields: Owner reserve increment: 0.2 XRP per object (mainnet, mid-2026). Base account reserve: 1 XRP. NFTokenPage capacity: up to 32 NFTs; rule-of-thumb ~24/page. Reserve estimate for N NFTs: (24N)/2 interpreted as ~N/12 XRP. Each open NFTokenOffer (sell or buy) also costs 0.2 XRP, recovered on accept/cancel. Pages are auto-created/consolidated by the protocol; burning that empties or consolidates a page reduces reserve by one increment. NFTs sort into pages by NFTokenID, so packing efficiency depends on ID distribution.
capabilities.gotchas: Reserve is locked, not spent — it returns when tokens leave the account or pages consolidate, but it is unavailable working capital meanwhile. A live sell offer per NFT doubles effective per-NFT cost during a drop (0.2 page-amortized + 0.2 offer). Reserve increments are governed by validator vote and could change; never hard-code 0.2 — read it from server_info/server_state. Packing is worst-case-fragmented when NFTokenIDs are spread out, so real reserve can exceed the N/12 estimate. The issuer (Owner of inventory) bears the reserve, not the eventual buyer — plan issuer-account funding accordingly.

capabilities.name: Eager (scripted) vs lazy (mint-on-demand) minting
capabilities.summary: Two minting strategies with opposite trade-offs. Eager/scripted minting pre-mints the whole collection on-ledger so provenance and serials exist before sale, but you carry the full ~N/12 XRP reserve for unsold inventory. Lazy/mint-on-demand keeps the sale off-ledger (signed offers/allowlist) and mints only at purchase time, so there is zero reserve for unsold supply and no wasted mints on items that never sell — at the cost of no pre-sale on-chain history. For a game with a large or uncertain-demand catalog, lazy minting is usually the capital-efficient default; eager minting fits curated, guaranteed-sellout drops where pre-mint provenance matters.
capabilities.key_fields: Eager: loop NFTokenMint over the catalog, fund issuer for full reserve, optionally create per-NFT sell offers (extra 0.2 XRP each). Lazy: hold an off-ledger record of intended NFTs (URI + taxon + transferfee + flags), and at purchase execute mint-then-transfer (mint, create Destination-locked sell offer, buyer accepts) — often via an authorized minter service. Decision inputs: collection size, expected sell-through, working capital, need for pre-sale provenance, gas/fee volume tolerance.
capabilities.gotchas: Lazy minting means metadata/flags are decided at sale time, so a bug locks every later mint into the wrong transferfee or missing tfTransferable — pin the mint template per item up front. Eager minting wastes reserve and the small mint fee on unsold tail items; for a 10k drop with 30% sell-through you've locked reserve on 7k dead NFTs. With lazy minting you cannot show buyers an on-chain rarity/serial before purchase. Either way, mint serials come from FirstNFTSequence+MintedNFTokens (see remint amendment) so 'reserved slot' numbering must be planned, not assumed sequential-from-1.

capabilities.name: Authorized minter (asfAuthorizedNFTokenMinter)
capabilities.summary: An account can delegate minting to another account so a hot 'minting service' wallet can issue NFTs on behalf of a cold issuer/brand account. The issuer sets asfAuthorizedNFTokenMinter via AccountSet with the NFTokenMinter field; the delegate then mints with NFTokenMint carrying the Issuer field set to the cold account. Royalties/transfer fees still attribute to the Issuer, and the minted NFToken's issuer is the cold account — not the hot signer. This is the standard production pattern for a studio: keep the brand/issuer key cold while a server-side hot key does the high-volume minting.
capabilities.key_fields: Setup: AccountSet { Account: issuer, SetFlag: asfAuthorizedNFTokenMinter (10), NFTokenMinter: <delegate> }. Mint: NFTokenMint { Account: delegate, Issuer: <issuer>, NFTokenTaxon, ... } signed by the delegate. Remove: AccountSet { ClearFlag: 10 } and omit NFTokenMinter. Only ONE authorized minter at a time per issuer. The authorized minter (and issuer) can also burn tokens that have tfBurnable set.
capabilities.gotchas: Exactly one authorized minter per issuer — you cannot fan out to multiple hot keys via this mechanism; rotate or use Tickets/sequence pipelining on the single delegate. The delegate temporarily 'owns' nothing of the issuer's, but it does hold any NFTs it mints to itself until transferred (and bears that reserve). Forgetting to set the Issuer field on NFTokenMint mints the NFT under the delegate's own account instead of the brand — a silent provenance error. Clearing the flag without omitting NFTokenMinter is a malformed transaction. Transfer-fee/royalty payouts go to Issuer, so the cold account must be set up to receive them.

capabilities.name: Mint-time flags & TransferFee (royalty) decisions
capabilities.summary: Every NFTokenMint locks in a set of permanent flags and an optional secondary-sale royalty (TransferFee) that can NEVER be changed after mint. The choices: tfTransferable (can the asset move between players at all — without it, only issuer<->holder transfers, which makes a non-tradeable bound item), tfBurnable (can the issuer burn it later, e.g. to retire/redeem an asset), tfOnlyXRP (restrict sale currency to XRP), and TransferFee (0.000%-50.000% royalty on secondary sales, requires tfTransferable). These flags ARE the asset's economic policy; choosing them wrong is unrecoverable except by burn+remint.
capabilities.key_fields: Flags: tfBurnable=1, tfOnlyXRP=2, tfTrustLine=4 (DEPRECATED), tfTransferable=8 (required for any 3rd-party trade and for any non-zero TransferFee), tfMutable=16 (mutable URI; requires DynamicNFT). TransferFee: UInt16, valid 0..50000 = 0.000%..50.000% in 0.001% steps; only valid when tfTransferable is set; paid to the Issuer on each secondary sale. Other fields: NFTokenTaxon (req), Issuer (when authorized minting), URI (<=256 bytes, hex), and optional Amount/Expiration/Destination for an auto-created sell offer at mint.
capabilities.gotchas: TransferFee and all flags are immutable post-mint — no NFTokenModify for these (NFTokenModify only touches URI of mutable NFTs). Setting TransferFee without tfTransferable is malformed and rejected. tfTrustLine is deprecated by fixRemoveNFTokenAutoTrustLine — do not set it. Forgetting tfTransferable produces a soulbound-style token that players can never trade on a marketplace (sometimes desired for bound gear, usually a mistake for collectibles). A 50% cap means you cannot encode a >50% sink via royalty. Royalties accrue to Issuer, so with authorized minting confirm the cold issuer is the fee recipient.

capabilities.name: Dynamic NFTs — mutable URI (NFTokenModify + tfMutable)
capabilities.summary: Live on mainnet since 2025-06-11, DynamicNFT lets an NFT minted with the tfMutable flag have its URI updated later via the NFTokenModify transaction. For games this enables evolving/stateful assets — gear that levels up, characters whose art/metadata changes, season-pass tokens that update — without burning and reminting (which would change the NFTokenID and break provenance). Mutability MUST be opted in at mint time with tfMutable; it cannot be added afterward, and only the URI is mutable (not flags, taxon, or transfer fee).
capabilities.key_fields: Mint with tfMutable (16). Modify via NFTokenModify { Account, Owner (if not the signer), NFTokenID, URI (new value, <=256 bytes hex; omit/empty to clear) }. Authorized to modify: the issuer and (per authorized-minter rules) the authorized minter — not arbitrary holders. Only the URI changes; the NFTokenID is stable, so off-ledger metadata at that URI is where the evolving game state lives.
capabilities.gotchas: If you didn't set tfMutable at mint, the NFT is permanently immutable — there is no retrofit. Only URI changes; you cannot mutate transfer fee, flags, or taxon, so 'dynamic stats' must live entirely in the off-ledger metadata document the URI points to. Mutation is an issuer/minter privilege, not the holder's, so a player cannot self-evolve their item — your game backend signs the NFTokenModify. Pointing the URI at mutable off-chain storage (HTTP) means provenance of past states isn't on-chain; use content-addressed (IPFS/arweave) snapshots if state history matters. Relatively new (2025) — confirm wallet/marketplace display support for updated URIs.

capabilities.name: NFTokenBurn — supply & sink mechanics
capabilities.summary: NFTokenBurn permanently removes an NFT from the ledger. The current holder can always burn their own token; the issuer (and its authorized minter) can also burn it only if it was minted with tfBurnable. For game economies this is the on-chain sink: consume a single-use item, redeem an asset for an in-game reward, retire deprecated gear, or run deflationary supply control. Burning also recovers reserve when it empties or consolidates an NFTokenPage.
capabilities.key_fields: NFTokenBurn { Account, NFTokenID, Owner (required when burning a token you don't hold, e.g. issuer burning a holder's tfBurnable token) }. Permission: holder always; issuer/authorized-minter only if tfBurnable set at mint. Effect: NFToken removed from its NFTokenPage; if the page empties/consolidates, owner reserve drops by one 0.2 XRP increment. Burn does NOT decrement the issuer's MintedNFTokens counter — minted-IDs keep advancing (see remint amendment).
capabilities.gotchas: tfBurnable is a permanent mint-time choice — if you want the issuer to be able to reclaim/retire player-held assets (redeem-to-burn, anti-cheat clawback), you MUST set tfBurnable at mint; you cannot add it later. Issuer burn of a holder's token is a real clawback power — disclose it, players may object to a collection where the issuer can destroy their assets. Burn is irreversible (no named compensator exists at protocol level — design redeem flows so the burn is the last, intended step). MintedNFTokens never decreases, so 'circulating supply' must be tracked as minted-minus-burned off-ledger, not read from one field.

capabilities.name: At-scale minting throughput — Tickets & sequence pipelining
capabilities.summary: Without atomic batches (the Batch/XLS-56d amendment is NOT enabled on mainnet as of mid-2026), high-volume minting relies on Tickets to submit many NFTokenMint transactions in parallel instead of strictly one-after-another by Sequence. A single account can pre-allocate up to 200 tickets at once, letting a minting service fire ~200 mints concurrently without sequence-ordering stalls. Reported NFT offer/accept workloads sustained ~751 ops/sec on the ledger, so throughput is rarely the bottleneck; reserve and orchestration are.
capabilities.key_fields: TicketCreate { TicketCount: up to 250 outstanding, with up to 200 created per group } pre-allocates ticket sequence numbers; each NFTokenMint then sets TicketSequence instead of Sequence so order-independence holds. Limits: 200 transactions in one parallel group; ~751/sec sustained NFT offer+accept throughput observed in RippleX testing. Tickets cost a 0.2 XRP reserve each until consumed. Standard fee per tx applies; budget XRP for fees across thousands of mints.
capabilities.gotchas: Tickets give parallelism but NOT atomicity — a 10k mint job can partially fail; you need idempotent retry keyed on TicketSequence and reconciliation against MintedNFTokens, not all-or-nothing. The Batch amendment that WOULD give atomic multi-mint was blocked: a signer-validation vulnerability was found 2026-02-19 and rippled 3.1.1 (2026-02-23) marked Batch + fixBatchInnerSigs unsupported — do not design around atomic batches on mainnet yet. Each outstanding ticket holds 0.2 XRP reserve, so 200 tickets temporarily locks 40 XRP on top of NFT reserve. Watch per-ledger load limits and fee escalation under burst submission.

capabilities.name: fixNFTokenRemint — NFTokenID derivation & issuer-deletion lock
capabilities.summary: fixNFTokenRemint changed how NFTokenIDs are generated so a deleted-and-recreated issuer account cannot mint a token that collides with a previously-issued NFTokenID. It introduces the AccountRoot field FirstNFTokenSequence (fixed at the account's sequence when it first mints) and computes each new token's sequence as FirstNFTokenSequence + MintedNFTokens. For a studio this matters for two reasons: serial numbers do not start at 1, and the issuer account becomes hard to delete after minting — a constraint to know before you architect issuer-account lifecycle.
capabilities.key_fields: FirstNFTokenSequence (AccountRoot, set once at first mint = account Sequence then). Token sequence = FirstNFTokenSequence + MintedNFTokens; MintedNFTokens increments per mint and never decrements (burns don't lower it). Account-deletion restriction: an issuer can only be deleted once FirstNFTokenSequence + MintedNFTokens + 256 < current ledger index. Implication: NFTokenID's sequence component is account-relative, not collection-relative.

research.notes: Mid-2026 depth synthesis on using XRPL primitives as game assets. XRPL gives you native, first-class NFTs (XLS-20, live on mainnet 2022-11-01) with no smart contract required, plus the newer DynamicNFT (XLS-46, enabled mainnet 2025-06-11) for mutable URI, and Multi-Purpose Tokens (XLS-33, the v2 fungible/semi-fungible standard) for fungible game items. The single most important architectural decision for a game economy is the NFT-vs-MPT-vs-IOU choice per item type: unique, individually-tracked assets (a named weapon, a land plot, a character) are NFTs; interchangeable stackable items (gold, potions, ammo, crafting mats, reputation points) should be MPTs, NOT NFTs — minting 5,000 identical 'health potion' NFTs is the canonical anti-pattern (~52 bytes/MPT holding vs an NFTokenPage per ~24 NFTs, and an owner reserve cost of roughly 1/12 XRP per NFT). Soulbound items use the absence of tfTransferable (achievements, identity, account-bound starter gear). Rarity/traits live in off-chain JSON metadata (XLS-24 community schema) referenced by the 256-byte URI, with NFTokenTaxon grouping a collection/series. Royalties are protocol-enforced via TransferFee (0-50%) — a genuine XRPL advantage over the broken approval-based royalty model on EVM chains. Real prior art on XRPL is real but modest: CryptoLand (play-to-earn strategy, land + avatar + equipment NFTs), Space Mermaids (first play-to-mint, Ripple Creator Fund), distribution via xrp.cafe and Sologenic. Cross-game interoperability remains mostly cosmetic/identity-level industry-wide ('Metaverse Light'), not functional stat-portability — design for it as a marketing surface, not a mechanic. Primary metadata risk is centralization: pin to IPFS/Arweave (or data-URL on-chain for tiny payloads), never a plain HTTP host you control.
